slides.heading: Population
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why the number of people has risen so fast, and how we measure it.

visual.alt: Flow: births and people moving in add to a population; deaths and people moving out reduce it

slides.narration: A population changes in only four ways. Babies are born, people die, and people move in or move out. In this part we see why births have far outnumbered deaths in the last century, and we learn how to measure a population with a few simple rates.

slides.narration: For most of history the human population grew very slowly. Then, in the last two centuries, the curve turned sharply upwards. Each new billion has arrived faster than the one before. A curve like this is called J shaped.

slides.heading: Why did the population explode?

headers: Birth rate stayed high because of
rows: Illiteracy; little knowledge of family planning
Children seen as help and support in old age
Wish for a son; social customs

visual.alt: Table of reasons why the death rate fell and why the birth rate stayed high

slides.narration: The explosion came from a gap. Medicine, food and clean water cut the death rate quickly. But the birth rate depends on customs and beliefs, which change slowly. So for many years, far more people were born than died.

slides.heading: Measuring a population: demography
slides.body_md: **Demography** is the statistical study of human populations.

rows: Live births per 1000 people in a year
Deaths per 1000 people in a year
(Birth rate − death rate) ÷ 10, in per cent a year (migration ignored)
Number of people per square kilometre

visual.alt: Table of four demographic terms and their meanings

slides.narration: Demographers use rates so that places of different sizes can be compared. Birth rate and death rate are counted per thousand people each year. Their difference, divided by ten, gives the growth rate in per cent. Density tells us how crowded the land is.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: rates for a town
slides.body_md: A town of **50,000** people had **1,100** births and **400** deaths in a year.
bullets: Step 3: growth rate = (22 − 8) ÷ 10 = **1.4 per cent** a year.

visual.alt: Worked table: birth rate 22, death rate 8, growth rate 1.4 per cent a year

slides.narration: Divide the births by the population and multiply by a thousand. Do the same for deaths. Then subtract, and divide by ten to turn a rate per thousand into a percentage. This town grows by 1.4 per cent a year.

slides.heading: Quick check: the study of populations
slides.body_md: Fill in: the statistical study of human populations is called ______.
slides.narration: The word begins with the Greek for people.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which district is more crowded?
bullets: Step 1: X = 12,00,000 ÷ 2,500 = **480** per square kilometre.
Step 2: Y = 10,00,000 ÷ 4,000 = **250** per square kilometre.
Step 3: X is more crowded, though it is smaller.

visual.alt: Worked table: district X has density 480 and district Y has density 250 people per square kilometre

slides.narration: District Y has more land, but District X packs more people into each square kilometre. Density is people divided by area, and it is the fair way to compare crowding.

slides.heading: Quick check: density
slides.body_md: True or false: population density is the number of people per square kilometre.
slides.narration: People divided by area.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Population explosion: the death rate fell sharply while the birth rate stayed high.
Demography is the statistical study of populations.
Birth rate and death rate are per 1000 people per year.
Growth rate = (birth rate − death rate) ÷ 10 per cent; density = people ÷ area.

visual.alt: Summary table of the units of the demographic rates

slides.narration: To recap. The population exploded because deaths fell faster than births. We measure a population with birth rate, death rate, growth rate and density, and each has its own unit.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always state the **unit**: per 1000 per year, per cent per year, or per square kilometre.
Growth rate uses **birth rate minus death rate**, never the sum.
Show each **step** of a calculation.
For real figures, quote the **source and year** (for example, Census 2011).
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write the unit with every rate. Subtract the death rate, do not add it. Show your working step by step. And when you quote a real figure, say where and when it comes from.

slides.heading: Problems and Control
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what happens when people outgrow their resources, and how growth can be slowed.

visual.alt: Flow: population explosion leads to unemployment, over-use of resources, low per capita income, price rise, pollution and unequal distribution of wealth

slides.narration: When a population grows faster than its food, water, jobs and homes, life becomes harder for everyone. In this part we look at the problems of a population explosion and at the ways a country can slow its growth.

slides.heading: Problems of population explosion

rows: Job-seekers grow faster than new jobs
Forests, water, soil and minerals used faster than renewed
Total income shared by more people
Demand for goods grows faster than supply
More vehicles, fuel, sewage and garbage
The gap between rich and poor widens

visual.alt: Table of six problems caused by population explosion and why each happens

slides.narration: Each problem has a simple cause. More people want more jobs, more food and more goods than the country can produce. Prices rise and incomes are spread thinly. More people also make more waste, and the gap between rich and poor grows.

slides.heading: Quick check: jobs
slides.body_md: Job-seekers grow faster than jobs. Which problem results?
slides.narration: Many people without work.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: per capita income
bullets: Step 1: with 2,000 people, per capita income = ₹6,00,00,000 ÷ 2,000 = **₹30,000**.
Step 2: with 2,500 people and the same income = **₹24,000**.
Step 3: each person is **₹6,000** poorer, though the village earns the same.

visual.alt: Worked table: per capita income falls from 30000 rupees to 24000 rupees when the population rises from 2000 to 2500

slides.narration: Per capita income is total income divided by the number of people. If the income stays the same while the population grows, every share becomes smaller. That is why rapid growth keeps incomes low.

slides.heading: Why control population?

rows: Resources last and are not over-used
Services can keep pace with the people
Higher per capita income; steadier prices

visual.alt: Table of four needs for population control and the benefit of slower growth

slides.narration: Population control does not mean having no children. It means slowing growth so that food, water, jobs, schools and hospitals can keep up, and everyone can enjoy a better quality of life.

slides.heading: Slowing growth without surgery

headers: How it lowers the birth rate
rows: Later marriage; smaller families by choice
Families learn the benefits of fewer children
When children survive, parents do not need many
Couples can space and limit births

visual.alt: Table of four measures that lower the birth rate without surgery and how each works

slides.narration: Most of the fall in birth rates comes from choices, not operations. When girls stay in school they marry later. When families see that their children survive and thrive, they choose to have fewer. Advice at health centres helps couples plan their families.

slides.body_md: **Vasectomy** (men): a small piece of each **vas deferens** is removed and the ends tied. **Tubectomy** (women): a small piece of each **oviduct** is removed and the ends tied.

slides.narration: Both operations are small and both block a tube. In a man, the tubes that carry sperms are cut and tied, so no sperms reach the semen. In a woman, the oviducts are cut and tied, so the egg cannot meet any sperm.

rows: Ovaries and uterus: eggs, hormones, menstruation

slides.narration: Notice what is not touched. After vasectomy the testes still make testosterone. After tubectomy the ovaries still make hormones and the monthly cycle goes on. Only the path of the gametes is blocked, which is why these methods are permanent.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Population explosion causes unemployment, over-use of resources, low per capita income, price rise, pollution and unequal wealth.
Control is needed so that resources and services keep pace with people.
Vasectomy: each vas deferens cut and tied. Tubectomy: each oviduct cut and tied.
Hormones and the menstrual cycle continue after these operations.

slides.narration: To recap. Too many people for too few resources brings many problems. Slowing growth helps everyone. And the two surgical methods block the path of sperms or eggs while leaving the hormone making organs untouched.

sections.heading: 1. Population explosion in India and the world
sections.body_md:
**Population explosion** is a very rapid increase in the number of people in a short time.

**The world:** about 1 billion people around 1804, 2 billion around 1927, and 8 billion around 2022 (approximate UN milestones). The first billion took all of human history; the step from 7 to 8 billion took only about 11 years. The growth curve is **J-shaped**.

**India (Census of India):** 36.1 crore in 1951 and 121.1 crore in 2011; between 2001 and 2011 the population rose by about 18.2 crore (17.7 per cent). India has about 2.4 per cent of the world's land area but a far larger share of its people.

**Main reasons**
- **Fall in death rate:** vaccines, antibiotics, safer childbirth, more food, clean water and sanitation; fewer infant deaths and longer life expectancy.
- **High birth rate:** early marriage, illiteracy, little awareness of family planning, children seen as helpers and support in old age, desire for a son, social and religious customs.

The death rate fell quickly while the birth rate fell slowly, so the **gap** between them, the growth, became very large.

key_terms.definition_md: A very rapid increase in population within a short time.
The average number of years a person is expected to live.

sections.heading: 2. Demography: density, birth rate, death rate, growth rate
sections.body_md:
**Demography** is the statistical study of human populations: their size, density, distribution, births, deaths and migration.

| Term | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Birth rate (natality) | Live births per 1000 people in a year | per 1000 per year |
| Death rate (mortality) | Deaths per 1000 people in a year | per 1000 per year |
| Growth rate | (Birth rate − death rate) ÷ 10, migration ignored | per cent per year |
| Population density | Population ÷ area | people per square km |

**Example:** a town of 50,000 with 1,100 births and 400 deaths has a birth rate of 22, a death rate of 8 and a growth rate of 1.4 per cent a year. A district of 12,00,000 people on 2,500 square km has a density of 480 per square km.

**Migration** (people moving in or out) also changes the size of a population.

key_terms.definition_md: Live births per 1000 people per year.
Number of people per square kilometre.

sections.heading: 3. Problems caused by population explosion
sections.body_md:
- **Unemployment:** the number of job-seekers grows faster than new jobs.
- **Over-exploitation of resources:** forests are cut, groundwater is over-pumped, soil is over-used, minerals and fuels are used up.
- **Low per capita income:** per capita income = total income ÷ population, so the same income shared by more people gives each less.
- **Price rise:** demand for food, housing and goods grows faster than supply.
- **Pollution:** more vehicles, factories, fuel, sewage and garbage pollute air, water and soil.
- **Unequal distribution of wealth:** the gap between rich and poor widens.
- Also: shortage of **housing** (slums), and crowded **schools, hospitals and transport**.

key_terms.definition_md: Total income of a country or place divided by its population.

sections.heading: 4. Need for population control; vasectomy and tubectomy
sections.body_md:
**Need for control:** to balance the population with land, water, food and jobs; to provide schools, health care and housing for all; to raise per capita income and the quality of life; to reduce pollution and the loss of forests. Education of girls, later marriage, awareness of the **small family norm** and family planning help to lower the birth rate.

**Surgical (permanent) methods**
- **Vasectomy (men):** a small piece of each **vas deferens** is removed and the cut ends tied. Sperms cannot pass into the semen. The testes go on making sperms and **testosterone**, so male characters are unchanged.
- **Tubectomy (women):** a small piece of each **oviduct** is removed and the cut ends tied. The egg cannot meet the sperms. The ovaries go on releasing eggs and **hormones**, and **menstruation continues**.

Both are chosen only by couples who want no more children, because the cut tubes are difficult to rejoin.

key_terms.definition_md: Cutting and tying of each vas deferens in men.
Cutting and tying of each oviduct in women.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the death rate to the birth rate to find the growth rate.
- Leaving out units (per 1000 per year, per cent, per square km).
- Saying the testes or ovaries are removed in vasectomy or tubectomy.
- Saying menstruation stops after tubectomy, or that testosterone stops after vasectomy.
- Quoting a population figure without its source and year.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a rate with its unit, an odd one out **with its category**.
- 2 marks: a calculation with working, or two reasons.
- 3 marks: three problems or three measures, each with a cause or an effect.

questions.stem_md: District X has 12,00,000 people on 2,500 square kilometres; District Y has 10,00,000 people on 4,000 square kilometres. Which district is more densely populated? Show your working.

answer.model_answer_md: X: 12,00,000 ÷ 2,500 = **480** per square kilometre. Y: 10,00,000 ÷ 4,000 = **250** per square kilometre. So **District X** is more densely populated, although it has a smaller area.

questions.solution_md: X 480, Y 250: X is denser.

questions.stem_md: If a country's total income stays the same while its population doubles, its per capita income will
questions.solution_md: Per capita income = total income ÷ population; doubling the divisor halves the result — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A rapidly growing population tends to push up prices mainly because

options.text_md: the demand for food and goods rises faster than their supply

questions.solution_md: When more people compete for limited goods, prices rise — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which problem arises when the number of people looking for work grows faster than the number of new jobs?
questions.solution_md: More job-seekers than jobs means many remain without work — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A forest near a growing town is cleared for houses and farms, and the nearby stream dries up in summer. This is an example of

options.text_md: over-exploitation of natural resources caused by population pressure

questions.solution_md: More people need more land, wood and water, so forests and water sources are used up — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A population explosion helps to share wealth more evenly among people.

**Reason (R):** In a population explosion, more people have to share limited resources.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: crowding usually makes the gap between rich and poor wider. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A shortage of housing in fast-growing cities leads to the growth of slums.
questions.solution_md: True. People who cannot afford houses crowd into slums with poor sanitation.

questions.stem_md: Give the term: the average income of a person, found by dividing the total income of a country by its population.

answer.model_answer_md: **Per capita income.**

questions.solution_md: Per capita income.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Unemployment, Price rise, Low per capita income, Better schools for all.

answer.model_answer_md: **Better schools for all**; the others are **problems caused by population explosion**.

questions.solution_md: Crowding strains schools rather than improving them.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: population explosion leads to unemployment.

answer.model_answer_md: The number of people of working age **grows faster than new jobs** can be created, so many people **cannot find work**.

questions.solution_md: Job-seekers outnumber jobs.

questions.stem_md: How does population explosion lead to over-exploitation of natural resources? Give two examples.

answer.model_answer_md: More people need more **food, water, fuel, land and timber**, so resources are used faster than they are renewed. Examples: **forests are cut** for farms and houses; **groundwater is over-pumped** and wells run dry.

questions.solution_md: Demand exceeds renewal; forests, water.

questions.stem_md: A village earns ₹6,00,00,000 in a year and has 2,000 people. Find its per capita income. What will it become if the population grows to 2,500 while the income stays the same?

answer.model_answer_md: Per capita income = ₹6,00,00,000 ÷ 2,000 = **₹30,000**. With 2,500 people it falls to ₹6,00,00,000 ÷ 2,500 = **₹24,000**, a fall of ₹6,000 per person.

questions.stem_md: Explain how population explosion leads to (a) a rise in prices, (b) more pollution and (c) unequal distribution of wealth.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Demand** for food, housing and goods rises faster than **supply**, so prices go up.
(b) More people use more **vehicles, fuel and goods** and produce more **sewage and garbage**, polluting air, water and soil.
(c) Those who own land and businesses gain, while the growing number of **poor** share very little, so the **gap between rich and poor widens**.

questions.solution_md: Demand and supply; waste and fuel; gap widens.

questions.stem_md: In vasectomy,

options.text_md: a small piece of each vas deferens is removed and the cut ends are tied
each oviduct is cut and tied

questions.solution_md: Cutting and tying the vas deferens stops sperms from reaching the urethra — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Tubectomy prevents pregnancy because

options.text_md: the egg cannot pass along the cut and tied oviducts to meet the sperms
no more eggs are formed in the ovaries

questions.solution_md: The ovaries still release eggs and hormones; the cut tubes keep the egg and sperms apart — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about a man who has had a vasectomy is correct?

options.text_md: His semen still contains sperms but they cannot swim
His testes still make sperms and testosterone, but his semen contains no sperms

questions.solution_md: Only the vas deferens is cut; the testes keep working, so hormones and characters are unchanged — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The main aim of population control in a country with a high growth rate is to

options.text_md: balance the population with the available resources and improve the quality of life
stop all people from moving between states

questions.solution_md: Control slows growth so that food, jobs, schools and health care can keep up — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the figure, which letter marks the site that is cut and tied in tubectomy?
questions.solution_md: C marks the cut oviduct. A is the cut vas deferens, D the ovary and E the uterus — option (d).

**Assertion (A):** Vasectomy is a permanent method of preventing conception.

**Reason (R):** In vasectomy the testes of the man are removed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true: the cut tubes are not normally rejoined. The reason is false: the testes are not removed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? After tubectomy, a woman stops menstruating.
questions.solution_md: False. The ovaries and uterus are untouched, so the cycle and menstruation continue.

questions.stem_md: The surgical method of birth control in women, in which a small part of each oviduct is removed and the ends tied, is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Tubectomy.

questions.stem_md: Give the term: the surgical method of birth control in men in which each vas deferens is cut and tied.

answer.model_answer_md: **Vasectomy.**

questions.solution_md: Vasectomy.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: vasectomy and tubectomy are chosen only by couples who do not want any more children.

answer.model_answer_md: They are **permanent** methods: the cut and tied tubes are **difficult to rejoin**.

questions.solution_md: Permanent.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between vasectomy and tubectomy, giving two points.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Vasectomy** is done on **men**; **tubectomy** on **women**.
2. In vasectomy each **vas deferens** is cut and tied, so sperms cannot reach the semen; in tubectomy each **oviduct** is cut and tied, so the egg cannot meet sperms.

questions.solution_md: Person; tube cut.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why population control is needed in a country like India.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Resources such as **land, water and food** are limited, and a fast-growing population uses them up.
2. A smaller rate of growth lets the country provide enough **jobs, schools, housing and health care**, raising the **standard of living**.

questions.solution_md: Limited resources; better quality of life.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) A testis with the **vas deferens** leading upwards; a short piece of the vas deferens removed and both ends **tied**. (b) The uterus with an **oviduct** on each side leading to an **ovary**; a short piece of each oviduct removed and both ends **tied**.

questions.solution_md: Two diagrams with the cut sites labelled.

The health office of a hill town recorded the following for one year:

| Item | Number |
|---|---|
| Population at the start of the year | 50,000 |
| Live births | 1,100 |
| Deaths | 400 |
| People who moved into the town | 300 |
| People who moved out | 100 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 22

**(b)** 8

**(c)** 1.4 %

**(d)** 50900

**(e)** 1. **Shortage of housing**, so slums grow on the hillsides.
2. **Shortage of water**, as springs and wells cannot supply everyone, and more sewage and garbage **pollute** the streams.
3. **Unemployment** and **rising prices**, as jobs and goods do not increase as fast as the number of people.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Birth rate $= \dfrac{1100}{50000} \times 1000 = 22$.

**(b)** Death rate $= \dfrac{400}{50000} \times 1000 = 8$.

**(c)** Growth rate $= \dfrac{22 - 8}{10} = 1.4$ per cent a year.

**(d)** 50000 + 1100 − 400 + 300 − 100 = 50900.

**(e)** Housing, water and pollution, jobs and prices.

**(b)** 2.5 %

**(d)** 1. **Education**, especially of girls, leads to later marriage and smaller families.
2. Families learn about **family planning** and the small family norm.
3. As fewer children die, parents no longer need many children for **support in old age**, and city living makes large families costly.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Vasectomy.**

**(b)** **Oviduct** (fallopian tube).

**(c)** Only the **vas deferens** is cut; the **testes (B)** are untouched and go on secreting **testosterone** into the **blood**, which keeps the male secondary sexual characters.

**(d)** The **ovaries (D)** still release eggs and secrete **oestrogen and progesterone**, so the **uterus (E)** still builds up its lining and sheds it each month. Only the **oviducts** are blocked.

**(e)** **Vasectomy:** sperms from the testes cannot pass the cut **vas deferens**, so the semen has **no sperms**. **Tubectomy:** the egg cannot pass the cut **oviduct**, so it **cannot meet any sperm** and fertilisation does not occur.

**(f)** (i) They are **permanent** methods. The cut tubes are **difficult to rejoin**, so the person may **not be able to have children** later.

**OR** (ii) 1. Its **land, water and food** are limited and are being used up faster than they are renewed.
2. Slower growth lets **jobs, schools, housing and health care** keep pace, so the **quality of life** improves.

**(b)** Oviduct.

**(c)** Testes still secrete testosterone into blood.

**(d)** Ovaries and uterus unaffected.

(ii) Limited resources; better life.

Express this rise as a percentage of the 2001 population (to one decimal place).

children.stem_md: Although the percentage growth each decade has slowed since 1991, the number of people added each decade has stayed very large. Why?

answer.model_answer_md: The percentage is applied to an **ever larger population**. Even a smaller rate of growth, applied to more than a hundred crore people, **adds many crore** each decade.

children.solution_md: Smaller rate on a larger base.

marking_scheme.step: Smaller rate still adds many people

children.stem_md: State two problems that such a large rise creates in Indian cities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Shortage of housing**, with the growth of crowded **slums**.
2. **Overloaded services**: traffic jams, shortage of water and power, and crowded schools and hospitals.

children.stem_md: Suggest three measures, other than surgical methods, that can help to slow population growth.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Education**, especially of girls, so that they marry later and choose smaller families.
2. **Awareness** of the **small family norm** and of family planning through health workers and the media.
3. Better **health care for mothers and infants**, so that parents do not feel they need many children for some to survive.

questions.passage_md: Two neighbouring villages, Sonpur and Ramgarh, each earned the same total income of ₹6,00,00,000 last year. Sonpur has 2,000 people; Ramgarh, where families are larger, has 2,500. Ramgarh's school has 60 children in each class, and its only well runs dry every May.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 30000

**(b)** 24000

**(c)** **Ramgarh.** The same income is shared by **more people**, so each person has **less money** for food, clothing, education and health care.

**(d)** With more children than the school was built for, classes of **60** mean **less attention** for each child. The **well runs dry** because more people draw more water than the rains put back, an example of **over-exploitation**. Another example: the village **health centre** becomes overcrowded, or nearby **trees are cut** for fuel.

**(e)** (i) 1. The advantages of a **small family**: more food, care and education for each child.
2. **Education of girls** and the legal age of marriage, so that they marry later.
3. Information on **family planning** methods available at health centres, including permanent methods for couples who want no more children.

**OR** (ii) 1. **Unemployment**, as farm land is divided into smaller plots that cannot employ everyone.
2. **Price rise** of food and land, as demand grows faster than supply.
3. **Pollution** of ponds and fields by more sewage and garbage.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** ₹6,00,00,000 ÷ 2,000 = 30000.

**(b)** ₹6,00,00,000 ÷ 2,500 = 24000.

**(c)** Ramgarh: lower per capita income.

**(d)** School, water, one more.

**(e)** (i) Small family, girls' education, family planning.

(ii) Unemployment, prices, pollution.
